common_name: Densa Walter's Viburnum (Dwarf Compact Florida Native Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Densa' stays compact enough for foundation plantings and low hedges without the size of the straight species.

directions: Set plants in well-drained, humus-rich soil and water regularly the first year to establish a dense, twiggy root system, after which 'Densa' handles both periodic drought and occasional wet spells common to Gulf Coast gardens. This naturally compact selection of the Florida native Walter's viburnum forms a tight, rounded mound of small, glossy, semi-evergreen leaves that need little pruning to hold a neat 4-to-5-foot shape, unlike the larger straight species. Clusters of small, fragrant white flowers open in late winter to early spring ahead of many other shrubs, drawing in early-season pollinators, and are followed by red berries ripening to black that songbirds strip through fall and winter. It takes light shade from taller trees without losing density and is an excellent low-maintenance evergreen hedge or screen for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast landscapes.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Whorled Class Walter's Viburnum (Compact Florida Native Hedge Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; space plants for a hedge or let them stand as a rounded specimen, since 'Whorled Class' holds a dense, uniform shape with little pruning.

directions: Grow in average garden soil with regular watering through the first year, after which this tough Florida native tolerates both dry spells and occasionally soggy ground. 'Whorled Class' takes its name from the distinctive whorled arrangement of three leaves per node along its stems, giving the dense, rounded shrub an unusually fine, textured look among viburnums. Lightly fragrant white flowers with buttery-yellow throats cover the plant from late winter into early spring, followed by red fruit that ripens to black and draws songbirds through the season. It handles heat, humidity, and light shade from overhead trees with ease, making it a reliable evergreen hedge or foundation shrub for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
JC Raulston Arboretum at NC State University

common_name: Beppu Virginia Sweetspire (Dwarf Suckering Native Groundcover Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Beppu' spreads by root suckers into a low, dense colony, making it well suited to mass planting or bank stabilization rather than tight single-specimen spots.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil and allow room to spread, since 'Beppu' suckers readily from the roots to form a low, dense colony rather than staying as a single clump. This compact selection of the native Virginia sweetspire tops out around 2 to 3 feet, shorter than most other named cultivars, and bears the same fragrant, drooping white flower spikes in early summer that draw bees and butterflies. Fall brings a rich wine-red to burgundy foliage color that holds well into the cooler months, even in mild Gulf Coast autumns. Its spreading habit and tolerance of wet, poorly drained soil make it a strong choice for erosion control on slopes or as a naturalizing groundcover shrub in partial shade.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Saturnalia Virginia Sweetspire (Multi-Color Fall Foliage Native Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Saturnalia' tolerates wet, periodically flooded ground and colors up reliably even in areas with mild autumns.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun and keep evenly watered, since this native sweetspire performs best where soil does not dry out for long. 'Saturnalia' was selected along the Wolf River in Tennessee for its exceptional fall display, in which individual plants can show simultaneous patches of gold, orange, and red rather than turning a single uniform color, and the display holds later into the season than many other sweetspire cultivars. In early summer it produces the same fragrant, arching, bottlebrush-like white flower spikes typical of the species, which are a strong draw for bees and butterflies. It spreads gradually by suckering into a loose colony over time, making it useful for naturalized plantings, rain gardens, and stream-bank stabilization in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast conditions.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; 'September Beauty' tolerates wet soils and extends the summersweet bloom season about a month later than most other cultivars.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade and mulch well, since summersweet suffers in dry conditions but thrives with damp roots. 'September Beauty' is valued for blooming roughly a month later than most other Clethra alnifolia selections, sending up dense, upright, 6-inch white flower spikes in late summer into September that fill the garden with a strong, sweet fragrance right as many other shrubs finish flowering. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit heavily during this late nectar flush, making it a valuable late-season pollinator resource. As an understory shrub it tolerates significant shade as long as soil moisture is maintained, and it may sucker gently over time to form a broader colony in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast plantings.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Blue Mist Dwarf Fothergilla (Blue-Foliage Bottlebrush Witch Alder)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Blue Mist' keeps its best steel-blue foliage color with some afternoon shade in hot Gulf Coast summers.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter and avoid letting the root zone dry out, since this dwarf witch alder relative struggles in poor, compacted ground. 'Blue Mist' is prized for its distinctive blue-gray summer foliage, a striking departure from the plain green leaves of the species, set off in early spring by small, fragrant, white bottlebrush-shaped flower spikes that open before the leaves emerge and draw in early bees. In fall the blue-toned leaves shift into a mix of orange, red, and yellow for a second season of strong color. This compact, slow-growing selection stays under 3 feet and works well massed at a woodland edge or foundation planting, and it has a track record of good garden performance recognized with a Pennsylvania Horticultural Society Gold Medal Award.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
